title: Real vs Fake Shilajit: How to Check Purity & Safety
description: Pure vs fake Shilajit: learn the home checks, the red flags, and why lab-tested Shilajit with a Certificate of Analysis is the only real proof of purity.
bodyHtml:
Shilajit has become popular fast, and popularity always brings imitations. If you have ever stared at two jars of black resin wondering which one is the real thing, you are asking the right question. Understanding pure vs fake Shilajit comes down to two separate issues that often get muddled together: is it actually Shilajit, and is it actually safe? A jar can pass the first test and still fail the second. Here is how to think about both honestly.

What fake Shilajit usually is

Most counterfeits are not random goo. The most common substitute is ozokerite, a naturally occurring mineral wax that is dark, sticky, and close enough in appearance to fool almost anyone on sight. Other adulterants include cheap resins, clay, humic-rich soil, and blends where a small amount of real Shilajit is stretched with fillers, colourants, or sweeteners.

The second category is trickier: Shilajit that is genuinely Shilajit, but unpurified. Raw material scraped from rock can carry heavy metals such as lead, arsenic, mercury and cadmium, along with microbial contamination. Some independent testing has also flagged thallium in a handful of products on the market. This is why proper purification and testing are not optional extras. They are the entire point of the process. If you want the background on how the raw material forms, our complete guide to Shilajit covers it.

Home checks: useful, but limited

Home tests can help you spot obvious fakes. They cannot tell you anything about safety. Treat them as a first filter, not a verdict.

  • The water test. Dissolve a pea-sized amount in warm water. Real resin should disperse fully, turning the water a deep reddish-brown or golden-black without chalky sediment or an oily film on top. Fillers tend to sink, float, or refuse to dissolve.
  • Texture and temperature. Genuine resin softens and becomes stretchy with warmth (in your hands or in a warm room) and firms up when cold. Ozokerite stays waxy and behaves more like candle wax than resin.
  • Smell and taste. Real Shilajit smells earthy, smoky, slightly like wet stone or old leather. The taste is distinctly bitter and mineral. Sweet, floral, or chemical notes suggest something has been added.
  • The flame check. Resin should bubble and smoulder rather than burn cleanly with a flame like wax. This one is messy and imprecise, so use it as a tiebreaker at most.

None of these will reveal lead at 3 parts per million. That is the honest limitation, and any brand telling you a kitchen test proves safety is skipping the part that matters.

The only real proof: lab-tested Shilajit

A Certificate of Analysis (COA) from an independent, accredited laboratory is the one piece of evidence that cannot be faked with clever branding. A meaningful COA shows:

  • Heavy metals screened individually, meaning lead, arsenic, mercury and cadmium, with results against a stated limit, not just a "pass" stamp
  • Microbial testing for bacteria, yeast, and mould
  • Fulvic acid content, so you know the active fraction is actually present
  • A batch or lot number that matches the jar in your hand, plus a recent test date

Ask for it. A brand that hesitates, sends a screenshot with the lab name cropped out, or shares a certificate from four years ago has answered your question. At Salxir we test every batch and are open about where our Shilajit comes from and how it is handled once it reaches Finland. That transparency is the product, as much as the resin is.

Red flags worth walking away from

Beyond the lab paperwork, a few patterns reliably separate serious brands from opportunists:

  • Vague origin. "Sourced from the Himalayas" is a region the size of a continent. Specificity signals a real supply chain.
  • Impossible pricing. Genuine purified Shilajit is labour-intensive to collect and process. Bargain-bin pricing usually means something else in the jar.
  • Medical promises. Claims that a supplement cures conditions or replaces medication are both a compliance problem and a credibility problem.
  • No batch traceability. If nothing on the packaging ties back to a specific production run, quality control is not being taken seriously.
  • Reviews that all sound alike. A wall of five-star, same-week, near-identical reviews is worth reading sceptically.

Does format change the purity question?

Not fundamentally. The testing standard should be identical whichever form you choose. Resin is the least processed option and lets you apply the sensory checks above yourself, which is part of why many people prefer it. Capsules, tablets and honey sticks trade that visibility for convenience and a much friendlier taste, so the COA does more of the work for you. If you are weighing the two, our breakdown of Shilajit resin vs capsules goes into the practical differences.

A simple buying checklist

Before you order, run through this: Can you see a recent third-party COA with heavy metals and fulvic acid listed? Does the batch number match? Is the origin described specifically? Does the price make sense for a hand-collected mineral resin? Are the health claims measured rather than miraculous? Five yeses and you are on solid ground.
